name: Zoe Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach piano from my flat most afternoons, fourteen pupils on an old upright I bought from a school that was closing. On Sundays I play the organ at St Columba's, the big church in the town centre, and I do the weddings and funerals there too. In spring I accompany children in their music exams, which means a lot of sitting in cold school halls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and the worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is when a pupil who's been stuck for months suddenly plays a piece through and looks up at me, astonished. The worst is the money, because no single part of it pays a proper wage. I live on my own above a dry cleaner, and I keep everything in a paper diary, which my pupils find hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and leave it there. I don't really post online. At church coffee after the service I'd probably say I never trusted the fuss anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my worries. My landlord put the rent up eight percent in September, and two families dropped lessons because they couldn't afford them. Even with AI as a flop, I'm one rent rise and two lost pupils away from not making the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a card up in the library and the supermarket for new pupils, which has always worked better than anything online. I'd ask the church council whether the organist's fee could go up, because it hasn't moved in six years. And I'd take on more exam accompanying in spring, even though it's exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and tired. Not panicking, but I lie awake doing sums some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said routine tasks get automated. Does any of your work feel routine like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam accompanying, a bit. A couple of schools already use recorded backing tracks for the lower grades, so I lost about six bookings last spring. That's two hundred and forty I'd counted on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the month doesn't add up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The piano tuning. I'd push it back three months and hope the pupils don't notice. Then I'd stop the gym, which I barely use anyway.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** and leave it there.
At **church coffee** I'd say I never trusted the fuss anyway.
think: My landlord's **eight percent** rent rise already squeezes me.
Two families **dropped lessons** this year because they couldn't afford them.
do: Put **cards** in the library and supermarket for new pupils.
Ask the church council to raise the **organist's fee**.
Take more spring **exam accompanying**, even though it's exhausting.
feel: **Uneasy** and tired, doing **sums** in bed some nights.
S0.quote: Even with AI as a flop, I'm one rent rise and two lost pupils away from not making the month.
fieldNote: AI Plateau barely touches her **worries**, which are rent and lost pupils.
Schools using **backing tracks** already cost her six bookings last spring.
She trusts **paper cards** over anything online to find pupils.

steps.text: Put cards in the library and supermarket for new piano pupils
Ask the church council to raise the organist's fee
Push the piano tuning back three months and cancel the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a real person at a funeral and a real teacher for their child, and I believe that. I'd keep it measured, because I know some parents use those apps already. I wouldn't sign petitions, but I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the exam accompanying goes completely, and some parents switch their children to a piano app that marks every wrong note. The church organ needs my hands on the keys, but my piano pupils' parents can buy an app for ten a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching the way I teach, but I'd offer cheaper group lessons for younger children on Saturday mornings in the church hall, so families who'd go to an app stay with me. I'd ask the vicar whether there's more funeral work at the two smaller churches nearby. I wouldn't touch the AI things myself; I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a way through. It's slower than the hype, and I'm slow too, so maybe we match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't know where to start with AI. Has anyone offered to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother Kwame keeps trying. He set something up on my phone once and I deleted it the next day. I'm not proud of that, but I like my paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a parent who said the app was good enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say an app can tell a boy he played a wrong note, but not why his shoulders are up round his ears. I'd say it politely. And then I'd probably lose them anyway.

I'd keep it **measured**, because some parents already use apps.
think: Parents can swap my lessons for a **piano app** at ten a month.
do: Run cheaper **group lessons** on Saturday mornings in the church hall.
Ask the vicar about **funeral work** at two smaller churches.
Stay away from **AI tools** and keep teaching her own way.
feel: **Anxious**, but she can see a **way through**.
S1.quote: The church organ needs my hands on the keys, but my piano pupils' parents can buy an app for ten a month.
fieldNote: She sees the **church organ** as safe hands-on work and **teaching** as exposed.
Her brother Kwame tries to help with **tech**, and she quietly undoes it.
She expects to lose some pupils even after arguing her case **politely**.

steps.text: Run cheaper Saturday group piano lessons in the church hall
Ask the vicar about funeral work at two smaller churches
Keep teaching individual pupils the same way, without AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, quietly, that I'm frightened, which isn't like me. At church I'd ask people to keep coming and keep asking for live music. I'd say the government needs to sort out some help for people, but I wouldn't know what exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means the apps become as good as a teacher at explaining things, and the exam work is long gone. My hands-on part lasts until 2031, but that's playing the organ for a congregation that's getting older and smaller. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two with no savings, playing hymns for forty people, and teaching whoever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move straight away to somewhere cheaper, maybe a shared house, because rent is the thing that would sink me. I'd ask at the care homes about playing for residents, which some of them pay for. I'd probably apply for a part-time job at the supermarket as well, so there's something regular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground is tilting. I'm not someone who moves quickly, and this would make me move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd share a house. Who with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe my cousin Ama, who's been asking. She's a nurse and works nights, so we'd hardly see each other. I've lived alone since college and I'd hate giving that up, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should help. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like help with rent while people find their feet, I suppose. I don't want a handout for life. I want a bridge.

say: At church I'd ask people to keep coming and keep asking for **live music**.
think: The **exam work** is gone, and apps explain things as well as I do.
By **2031** I'd be playing hymns for forty people with no savings.
do: **Move** somewhere cheaper, probably sharing with my cousin Ama.
Ask **care homes** about paid music sessions for residents.
Apply for a **part-time supermarket** job for something regular.
feel: Like the **ground is tilting**, forcing a slow person to move quickly.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be thirty-two with no savings, playing hymns for forty people, and teaching whoever's left.
fieldNote: Rent is the thing she fears will **sink** her, so moving comes first.
Her congregation is **ageing and shrinking**, so even the safe organ work is thin.
She wants a **bridge**, not a handout, which fits her middle-ground views.

steps.text: Move into a shared house with her cousin Ama
Offer paid music sessions to local care homes
Apply for a part-time job at the supermarket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them panicking. I'd suggest the church run more concerts, so there's a reason for people to come and hear live music. I'd say it in the parish newsletter, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years doesn't help me as much as it should, because I'm slow to change. If I had five years' warning, I'd probably spend four of those years hoping the warning was wrong. Meanwhile the teaching would thin out year by year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I made myself do it, I'd train as a music therapist, working with people with dementia or children with special needs. That's two years part-time and maybe four thousand, which I haven't got, so I'd need a loan. Meanwhile I'd keep the church and the pupils who stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, and a bit ashamed of myself for saying I'd wait. I know it's not sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing pupils, I think. If I went below ten, I'd have to. Or my brother Kwame sitting me down with the application form, which he would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why music therapy, and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's still sitting next to someone with music, and it's people at their most fragile. I don't think anyone wants a machine for that. I could be wrong, but it's the one thing I'd believe in.

say: We have **five years**, so let's not waste them panicking.
The church could run more **concerts** to bring people to live music.
think: Five years helps less than it should, because I'm **slow to change**.
I'd spend most of the warning **hoping** it was wrong.
do: Train as a **music therapist**, two years part-time for about four thousand.
Take a **loan** for the training, since I have no savings.
Keep the **church post** and remaining pupils meanwhile.
feel: **Heavy**, and a bit **ashamed** of wanting to wait.
S3.quote: If I had five years' warning, I'd probably spend four of those years hoping the warning was wrong.
fieldNote: She's unusually **honest** that she'd waste most of the warning time.
Dropping below **ten pupils** is her real trigger to act.
**Music therapy** appeals because it stays human and hands-on.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year part-time music therapy course
Hold off applying until pupils drop below ten
Keep the Sunday organ post at the town-centre church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to make a plan, including me. I'd encourage the parents I teach to keep their children playing, because music's worth it whatever happens. And I'd say the church and the council should keep funding live music in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven. My hands-on work, the organ and teaching little ones, goes on until about 2039. With ten years even a slow person like me can retrain, and I'd rather be a slow starter than a sorry one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the music therapy course over three or four years, part-time, paying as I go instead of taking a loan. I'd keep teaching and the church throughout. And I'd try to save twenty or thirty a month, starting with the money I spend on taxis home from late funerals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still worried about rent, but less like I'm running for a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools in the meantime, with ten years to get used to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the boring bits, like the exam board's paperwork, if Kwame showed me slowly. I'd still keep the paper diary. Some things you don't hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at home that changes with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to buy a small place one day, a flat with room for the piano. With two years I'd forget it. With ten I'd at least keep the dream on the fridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I don't move fast and that one doesn't give anyone time. What would help is help with rent for a year or two while people retrain, and grants for courses like music therapy, so people like me don't need loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm lonely, oddly. My piano pupils are half my social life, and if an app takes them, I lose my Tuesday conversations as well as my rent money.

headlineQuote: My piano pupils are half my social life, and if an app takes them, I lose my Tuesday conversations as well as my rent money.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old church organist** and piano teacher who lives alone above a dry cleaner.
She teaches **fourteen pupils**, accompanies exams and has almost **no savings**.
She **never uses AI** and keeps a paper diary, despite her brother Kwame's efforts.
She's measured and **middle-ground**, wanting a bridge for workers rather than handouts.
Her answer to longer warnings is **music therapy**, though she admits she'd wait too long.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she moves slowly and it gives no time.
whatWouldHelp: Help with **rent** for a year or two while people retrain.
**Grants** for courses like music therapy, so she wouldn't need loans.
